title: Edge proxy, MTU & quantization latency tuning for private VPC
summary: Deep technical session on private VPC deployment performance. Covered MTU/MTU blackholing, edge proxy hairpinning, DNS egress, PrivateLink termination, KV cache locality, batching/quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps for a 1-hour benchmark with jumbo frames, and a pilot network config to test hairpin NAT performance.
topics: KV cache locality and warm vs cold starts
next_steps: Ethan to share MTU tuning playbook and iperf samples by 2027-09-17
Customer to run 1-hour latency bench with q4-bit quantized model and MTU 9000 and report p50/p95 by 2027-09-22
Schedule on-prem lab session to test hairpin NAT and egress proxy with Redwood private deployment (target week of 2027-09-27)
Priya to provide suggested batching configs for 128/256 token payloads and recommended kv-cache TTLs
action_items: Ethan Park | share MTU playbook + iperf/netperf examples | 2027-09-17
Jules Park | run baseline bench (MTU 1500) and upload logs | 2027-09-18
Priya Nair | create recommended batching + kv-cache config gist | 2027-09-19
Maria Chen | validate split-dns resolver behavior in staging and share results | 2027-09-22
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-14 16:00 UTC | Duration: 78m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood), Alex (Nimbus VP Infra), Maria (SRE Lead), Darren (Security), Jules (ML Eng)

Summary: quick deep dive to surface networking hotspots for private-vpc deployment; focus on MTU, hairpin/eproxy behavior, dns and kv cache locality and how quantization changes token throughput.

[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, uh quick roll call, we got Alex, Maria, Darren, Jules from Nimbus and on our side Priya, Liam and myself. sound right?
[00:12] Alex: yep that's right, thanks Ethan. we wanted a very practical session — we've been seeing intermittent p95 spikes when requests come from the edge through our proxy into the private deployment.
[00:22] Priya: ok great, can you descr — describe the path quickly, like edge proxy -> nat -> privatelink -> inference nodes? any hairpinning in there?
[00:32] Maria: yeah so high level: external clients -> our edge egress proxy (in azure front door-ish) -> internal NAT gateway -> privatelink endpoint in our VPC -> then we have a subnet with the inference fleet. we also sometimes have internal services call the same endpoint and that does hairpin back through the proxy.
[00:51] Liam: hairpinning + small mtu mismatches often the cause of weird retransmits; curious what MTU you run on the infra side.
[00:58] Maria: default 1500; we tried jumbo frames in a dev AZ but saw flakiness. not sure if it was misconfigured or something else.
[01:06] Priya: ok that aligns. quick thing: our runtime is sensitive to per-packet latency for small token responses — if there's retransmits or fragmented packets it inflates p95. also kv cache lookups are network-bound if the cache is remote.
[01:22] Jules: when you say kv cache remote what do you mean? we currently keep the cache in a redis cluster over the VPC but not co-located with the inference machines.
[01:30] Priya: yeah that is exactly a common pattern — redis on a different AZ or subnet. every cache miss => additional RTT. when you have many short-turn requests (e.g., chat with short replies) that overhead is a big portion of latency.
[01:44] Darren: security question — we need to ensure KMS keys never cross outside our control. can privatelink be terminated on-prem? like for our air-gapped setup?
[01:53] Ethan: we support private deployments with customer-managed KMS and can run the control plane in your VPC or on-prem package. For privatelink specifically you can terminate at an NVA or at the privatelink endpoint. Priya can show options.
[02:04] Priya: yep two patterns: terminate privatelink at an internal NLB and do IP targeting into the inference subnet, or terminate at a proxy/NVA appliance that handles SNI passthrough and mTLS. each has tradeoffs for latency and session affinity.
[02:16] Alex: tradeoffs being?
[02:18] Priya: if you terminate at NLB -> straight TCP to pods, minimal extra hop. if you route via a proxy NVA for SNI/mTLS you add a hop and polymerizes TLS, which increases CPU and latency, but gives you centralized mTLS termination and easier audit.
[02:32] Maria: we observed CPU spikes on the proxy during bursts, which lined up with token generation phases.
[02:39] Liam: that probably means the proxy is doing TLS decrypt/encrypt per request; if your requests are chatty, that CPU cost and extra RTT matter. also consider TLS session resumption and keep-alive tuning.
[02:50] Jules: is Redwood doing any persistent connection pooling or connection reuse to the privatelink endpoints?
[02:55] Priya: yes our runtime uses connection pools and keeps HK/TCP alive to backend endpoints. but if the proxy kills idle connections or NAT timeouts exist you can still get reconnect overhead.
[03:06] Alex: we've got a 60s idle timeout on our proxy currently. could that be causing rehandshakes?
[03:10] Priya: definitely. handshake time for TLS can be tens of ms; multiplied by many small requests it adds up. increase keep-alive or enable session tickets/session resumption.
[03:19] Maria: ok. let's talk MTU — we tried 9000 but the infra team said many paths still had 1500 and fragmentation happened.
[03:27] Ethan: classic. mtu mismatch leads to fragmentation or blackholing. first step is to identify the smallest MTU along path using tcpdump and MTU discovery. what's your id procedures?
[03:36] Alex: we haven't instrumented MTU hops; we rely on cloud provider docs.
[03:40] Priya: we recommend a quick test: set the inference node with 9000, enable jumbo frames on your subnet if the cloud provider supports it, and run iperf and ping with don't-fragment to identify the path MTU. also inspect ALB/NLB and any transit gateways — some drop jumbo frames.
[03:56] Maria: ok we'll do that. what improvement should we expect?
[03:59] Priya: for generative workloads that send many tokens in small frames, moving from 1500 to 9000 can reduce CPU and per-token latency because you avoid fragmentation and fewer packets per response. But the biggest uplift is when your egress path is homogenous for MTU. If any link in the path breaks it results in fragmentation and retransmits.
[04:16] Jules: curious about quantization: we were planning to move to 4-bit quant for production. does that interact with network behavior?
[04:23] Liam: quantization primarily affects compute and memory bandwidth — lower-precision models produce tokens faster and reduce per-token CPU/GPU time. That increases request rate which increases the importance of connection reuse and batching. So network becomes the new bottleneck if compute drops.
[04:37] Priya: exactly. we often see throughput improve with quantized runtimes but p95 latency stays the same or worsens if your network or proxy can't handle the higher qps. So you have to tune batching, kv-cache TTLs, and network concurrency limits together.
[04:50] Alex: can you recommend batching settings for a short chat scenario? our median token response is 24 tokens.
[04:56] Priya: for short responses we recommend low-latency batching: target batch sizes of 2-8 requests with a time-window of 6-12ms for eager flush. use dynamic batch thresholds where if a request waits longer than threshold you flush. also keep per-worker concurrency limited so you don't thrash GPU memory and cause queueing.
[05:14] Jules: and kv cache? TTLs?
[05:16] Priya: if your workload is chatty with reuse of prefixes, warm caches with longer TTL like 10-30s. but if privacy/regulations require nothing cached, you'll need local on-host caches or pin cold-start warmers.
[05:28] Darren: on privacy, caches must be encrypted at rest and logs scrubbed; can Redwood integrate with our HSM?
[05:34] Ethan: yes we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations for private deployments, and we can disable persistent KV caching if required, or use in-memory per-instance caches only.
[05:43] Maria: ok. about DNS: our staging uses internal resolvers that implement split-horizon, sometimes the privatelink DNS returns different ips depending on source. we've seen timeouts when calls originate from containers behind the proxy.
[05:55] Priya: split-horizon/different resolvers cause inconsistent client routing; you want the inference nodes to use the same resolver as the privatelink endpoint so the returned IPs are routable. verify resolver configs in both host and container (nsswitch, resolv.conf) and consider pinning the privatelink endpoint IPs in host route for the inference subnet if DNS is flaky.
[06:16] Alex: good point. we'll audit our resolvers.
[06:20] Jules: can Redwood ship a small script to check DNS consistency and hairpin loops?
[06:24] Ethan: yes we'll include a small diagnostics script in the playbook.
[06:27] [pause/chatter]
[06:45] Priya: I want to call out a specific hairpin scenario we've debugged before: internal services call the public FQDN which resolves to the proxy VIP, that sends it to the proxy which then routes through the NAT back to the privatelink endpoint. That causes double NAT and source IP rewriting which can make affinity and connection reuse break. Have you seen source-IP rewriting?
[07:05] Maria: yes NAT translation was interfering with our source-based ACLs; we had to add SNAT exceptions but it's brittle.
[07:12] Priya: if possible, use split-dns for internal callers to hit the privatelink-alias directly and avoid hairpin altogether. If split-dns isn't an option, use direct VPC routing or internal-only LB that bypasses the proxy for internal flows.
[07:28] Alex: is there an easy fallback if we can't modify DNS?
[07:31] Liam: you can implement an edge proxy rule to bypass for internal subnets based on source IP ranges; or you can deploy a local envoy sidecar that rewrites and uses keep-alive pooling directly. Both add ops but avoid double NAT.
[07:45] Jules: let's talk numbers — if we enable 4-bit quant and batch aggressively, what p50/p95 numbers are realistic for 256-token requests?
[07:54] Priya: rough ballpark from similar customers: for 256 tokens with q4 quant and medium batching you might see p50 in the 80-120ms range and p95 ~300-500ms depending on network. If network has packet loss or fragmented frames p95 can jump to 800ms+.
[08:10] Maria: that's a wide range. we need stable p95 under 400ms.
[08:14] Priya: then prioritise network homogeneity (MTU, keep-alive), bring kv cache local, and limit burst qps with token bucket shaping at the proxy to smooth spikes. Also use canary rollouts and perf SLO alerts in Redwood Console.
[08:28] Darren: auditability remains key — if we offload TLS to a third party NVA do we lose traceability?
[08:34] Ethan: you can do TLS passthrough with SNI routing and still get request-level logs at the application layer. If the proxy terminates TLS you need to ensure logs include sanitized identifiers and we can tie that back to your audit trail.
[08:49] Alex: about benchmarking: what artifacts do you recommend we gather?
[08:53] Priya: capture p50/p95/p99 token latency, packet-level tcpdump at inference host and proxy during bench, iperf/netperf results for MTU tests, TLS handshake times, connection churn metrics, KV cache hit ratio, and CPU utilization on the proxy and inference nodes.
[09:07] Jules: ok we'll gather those.
[09:10] Ethan: quick demo of a small runbook: i'll share the MTU script, a tcpdump filter set, and a simple k6 script to ramp to 2x expected qps while measuring latencies.
[09:20] Maria: will you also share the recommended envoy config for connection pooling?
[09:24] Priya: yes we'll include a tuned envoy sample: increased http2 concurrent streams, longer keepalive, tuned keepalive timeouts, and backpressure settings.
[09:34] Alex: any gotchas for private link health checks? we saw health check flapping after we changed subnets.
[09:40] Liam: many health check flaps are due to source IP changes from NAT or firewall rules that block the provider's health probe IPs. Ensure security groups allow the privatelink health-source ranges and keep health check intervals aligned with readiness probes on the pods.
[09:54] Darren: threat modeling — if we pin MTU or use jumbo frames, does that open any fingerprinting or DoS surface?
[10:01] Priya: nothing unique to MTU itself, but operationally larger frames mean attacks that send large packets could amplify. Your network ACLs and rate limiting should handle that. Also, jumbo frames require consistent infrastructure config; misconfig yields outages rather than new attack vectors.
[10:18] Jules: for the lab benchmark, do you recommend on-host redis or redis cluster in same AZ?
[10:23] Priya: best is co-located on the same host or at least same AZ and using unix-domain-socket local caches if possible. If you must use redis cluster, ensure it is in the same AZ and tune socket buffers for high qps.
[10:35] Maria: how about fallback logic on Redwood? if a model variant is down or slow can it fall back to a smaller quantized model?
[10:41] Ethan: yes Redwood runtime supports model variant routing and automatic fallback policies. You can configure a fast small model as cold fallback and route based on latency thresholds or error rates.
[10:52] Alex: and cost implications? more local caching and larger MTU configs — any cost tradeoffs?
[10:57] Priya: jumbo frames don't directly cost more. More cache nodes and co-located infra increase instances but you save on per-token compute by improving throughput. It's a capacity vs net/infra tradeoff; we can model cost in the pilot.
[11:09] Maria: ok concrete plan?
[11:12] Ethan: timeline: this week we share playbook and scripts (Ethan), customer runs baseline benches (Jules/Maria), next week we reconvene with logs and we run a controlled canary with q4 quant and MTU 9000 in a single AZ. If we see regressions we fall back to 1500 and adjust keepalives.
[11:29] Alex: sounds good. can we also include the SRE on-call to avoid flapping during bench?
[11:33] Maria: yes i'll schedule the bench window off-peak.
[11:36] Priya: last note — instrument KV cache hit metrics at request-level so you can correlate p95 spikes to cache misses. also set alerts for connection churn on the proxy.
[11:47] Darren: for compliance we'll need a short write-up about where keys live and the caching behavior for auditors.
[11:53] Ethan: we'll include that in the handoff doc.
[11:56] Alex: great thanks everyone.
[12:00] Ethan: recap of next steps — i'll email the playbook and tests. Priya will send envoy/keepalive configs. Jules and Maria run bench and upload logs. we meet back on 2027-09-22 to review.
[12:14] Alex: thanks. end.

Notes on transcript: occasional filler and slight mislabels; audio-based ASR may have merged some names. Scripted artifacts will be attached to the calendar invite.
file_notes: Diagnostics + playbook to be attached by Redwood. Customer asked for on-host redis and envoy examples. Meeting was technical and SE-led, AE coordinated follow-ups.
